item.title: DuraShare: BIP39-native secret sharing with full manual fallback
item.description: Splits a BIP39 wallet seed into shares with Shamir secret sharing over F₂₀₅₃, with checksums against transcription errors and a MAC against tampering, so that the shares can be recovered by hand with paper and a calculator.

Arthur studies everlasting privacy in shielded pools such as Tornado Cash: whether a deposit stays unlinkable even to an attacker decades from now, with far more computing power or a quantum computer. He is building a variant whose deposits stay hidden even then, and measuring what that change costs.

Gabriel works on cryptography, blockchain, and distributed systems, implementing protocols in Rust and exploring zero-knowledge proofs for verifiable machine learning. He also uses Lean to formalize cryptographic constructions, connecting mathematical foundations with practical implementation.

Lionel studies zero-knowledge proofs applied to Bitcoin, in particular BitVM, which lets Bitcoin check arbitrary computations without changing the protocol. He is also studying MPC-in-the-head and VOLE-based proofs, and how they are used in FAEST, a post-quantum signature scheme.

Lucas studies privacy in zkVMs: which systems really hide the user’s data, rather than only producing short proofs. This semester his work was theoretical, from the definition of zero-knowledge to how today’s zkVMs obtain it. Next semester he will measure how practical it is, including on a phone.

Luiz studies commitments that hide the committed value unconditionally, even against unlimited computing power, while binding rests on hard problems from coding theory, which are believed to resist quantum computers. His starting point is HQC, the code-based scheme recently selected for standardization by NIST.

item.title: About Us
item.description:
ZKBR is a research group at the Department of Computer Science of the Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais (DCC/UFMG), Brazil. We study zero-knowledge proofs and the cryptography around them.

Our main focus is zero-knowledge virtual machines (zkVMs): how they work, how fast they are, and what they make possible, from scaling blockchains to proving facts about private data, such as transactions in central bank digital currencies or the provenance of edited images. A second line is zero-knowledge machine learning (zkML): proving that a model produced a given output, or was trained as claimed, without revealing the model or the data. We also follow the arrival of quantum computers and the new post-quantum algorithms, and what they mean for the proof systems and protocols we work with.
